newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Optimism grows as EU treaty talks gather pace.
newsitem.headline: Optimism grows as EU treaty talks gather pace.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers said on Tuesday they were more optimistic of agreeing landmark treaty reforms at an Amsterdam summit in four weeks after narrowing their differences on several key issues.

"There are fewer problems and we have shed more light on others, so they are more suitable for treatment," Dutch Foreign Minister and current EU president Hans van Mierlo told reporters after the foreign ministers met.

"There are about 15 points out of more than 100 that still have to be cleared up," Germany's Klaus Kinkel said. "I can imagine we'll make good progress on these on Friday. There will then remain a few points to be done at Amsterdam."

EU heads of state and government are due to meet in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk on Friday for a half-day informal session to gauge the chances of a successful outcome to an 18-month inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review, due to be completed at an Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.

The IGC, designed to prepare for future enlargement that could boost bloc membership beyond two dozen within a decade, has been largely overshadowed by the EU's ambitious plan to forge a single currency to vie with the dollar and yen on global financial markets,
Van Mierlo said all member states had reacted positively to an almost complete draft treaty prepared by The Netherlands, but warned that a full draft would not be ready until early June.
"There is a degree of optimism that a positive result will be achieved in Amsterdam," he said.

"But a great deal of work still needs to be done," he added, referring particularly to thorny issues such as merging the Western European Union (WEU) defence arm into the mainstream EU, a plan strongly opposed by Britain and the four neutral states -- Ireland, Sweden, Austria and Finland.
Although the issues at stake are themselves relatively mundane, the overall package is aimed at creating a more open and efficient bloc.
One EU diplomat said that around 90 percent of a new treaty was in place, leaving the dozen or so most contentious issues to be thrashed out by EU leaders between now and the June summit.

The outstanding issues include the new treaty's centrepiece; the creation by 2002 of an area of freedom and security, lifting all internal borders except those around Britain and Ireland, and taking a firm stand against organised crime, drug trafficking and illegal immigration.

Member countries must also work out how to streamline the bloc's decision-making processes, diluting the national veto with fewer areas requiring unanimity and re-weighting the voting structure in favour of larger EU countries.
Similarly, moves to give a higher profile to jobs and the environment must still be agreed, as is a form of flexibility to let some states forge ahead and integrate faster than others.
Existing procedures for agreeing common foreign and judicial policies are also expected to be strengthened.

While forthcoming elections in France and Ireland lend an air of uncertainty to the Amsterdam talks, the arrival of a more pro-European British government has significantly increased the mood of optimism in Europe.

The demise of the former Conservative administration, which fiercely opposed many issues favoured by its partners and threatened to block the treaty, was widely seen as removing the biggest obstacle to a meaningful agreement in Amsterdam.

"I do not come to Holland like Conservative ministers before me to try and wreck a deal. I come to try and get a deal -- a good deal for Britain and a good deal for Europe," British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told a news briefing.
